 1                III.    JURISDICTIONAL ALLOCATION FACTORS

 2   Q.   Please describe SPS’s need for jurisdictional allocation factors.

 3   A.   SPS maintains retail operations in New Mexico and Texas, and it has wholesale

 4        operations regulated by the Federal Energy Regulation Commission (“FERC”).

 5        Because a multi-jurisdictional utility such as SPS incurs joint and common costs to

 6        provide electric service to its customers across jurisdictions, it is necessary to

7         allocate such costs among those jurisdictions to develop consistent, just, and

8         reasonable rates. In determining the utility’s revenue requirement associated with

9         a jurisdiction, the jurisdictional allocation factors are multiplied by the utility’s

10        relevant costs to calculate the portion of such costs for which the specific

11        jurisdiction is responsible.

12   Q.   Are you the only SPS witness who addresses the jurisdictional allocation

13        factors?

14   A.   Yes. However, SPS witness Ms. Allison M. Johnson supports the jurisdictional

15        cost of service model. I provide Ms. Johnson with the New Mexico retail, Texas

16        retail, and firm wholesale allocation factors for production and transmission

17        capacity-related costs. Those are based upon monthly demands at the SPS system

18        peak. In addition, I provide Ms. Johnson with the New Mexico retail, Texas retail,

 1        and firm wholesale shares of line-loss-adjusted shares of energy forecasted to be

 2        consumed during the Future Test Year (“FTY”), which runs from December 1,

 3        2026 through November 30, 2027. She uses those fundamental allocation factors,

 4        as well as others she derives, to determine the New Mexico retail jurisdictional

 5        revenue requirement. Additionally, there are items directly assigned to the New

 6        Mexico jurisdiction proposed in Ms. Johnson’s testimony.

 7   Q.   How does SPS allocate costs among its customer jurisdictions?

 8   A.   For items that are not directly assigned to a specific jurisdiction, SPS develops three

10        jurisdictions—New Mexico retail, Texas retail, and firm wholesale requirements

11        customers:

12            (1)    a line-loss-adjusted kilowatt-hour (“kWh”) energy allocation factor for the

14                   maintenance (“O&M”), depreciation, taxes, and other costs;

15            (2)    a line-loss-adjusted production-related 12-CP 2 demand allocation factor (12
16                   CP Production Demand Allocation) for the allocation of production rate
17                   base, O&M, depreciation, taxes, and other costs; and

18            (3)    a line-loss-adjusted transmission-related 12-CP demand allocation factor
19                   (12 CP Transmission Demand Allocation) for the allocation of transmission
20                   rate base, O&M, depreciation, taxes, and other costs.

 3   Q.   What line-loss factors did you apply to the demand and energy data to

 4        establish the jurisdictional allocation factors?

 5   A.   The line-loss factors used were developed using data for calendar year 2021. The

 6        line-loss factors are described and listed in Schedule P-9 and were accepted by the

 7        Commission in Case No. 22-00286-UT. SPS is not proposing a new line-loss study

 8        in this case because: (1) there have been no significant changes to the transmission

 9        system; and (2) no new generation has been added to the SPS system that

10        significantly impacts power flows. SPS will evaluate and consider a new line-loss

11        study as new transmission and generation comes online in the coming years.

12   Q.   Please explain the 12-CP approach that SPS uses in allocating demand, or

13        capacity-related, costs to New Mexico retail customers.

14   A.   Under the 12-CP approach, each jurisdiction’s demand, coincident with the system

15        peak for each of the 12 months of the FTY, is used in allocating demand or capacity-

16        related costs to New Mexico retail customers. New Mexico and Texas retail

17        jurisdictional monthly peaks are determined by totaling the forecast of customer

18        class demands coincident with the SPS system peak in each jurisdiction for each


                                               8

                                        Taylor J. Hurt

 1        month.    Wholesale monthly peaks are similarly determined, by totaling the

 2        forecasted monthly production and transmission demands provided to those

 3        customers coincident with the SPS system peak on a firm basis. The monthly

 4        system peaks for each jurisdiction are then averaged, which is referred to as 12-CP.

 5        SPS determines New Mexico’s retail allocation by dividing the jurisdiction’s 12-CP

 6        by the 12-CP of the SPS system.

 7   Q.   How are the jurisdictional monthly peaks determined?

 8   A.   SPS forecasts the monthly wholesale and retail peaks coincident with the SPS

 9        system peak. Because SPS provides retail and wholesale service in both New

10        Mexico and Texas through a shared production and transmission system, the overall

11        forecasted production and transmission costs are allocated across the retail

12        jurisdictions in both states and are combined with the wholesale forecast to

13        determine the respective jurisdictional percentages of production capacity,

14        transmission capacity, and energy production costs included in base rates. For retail

15        customers, the allocation is determined for July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025

16        (“Base Period”) from load-research-based census and non-census monthly retail

17        customer class load factors applied to monthly kWh for each customer class. For

 1        the FTY Period (December 1, 2026 through November 30, 2027) a forecasted 8760

 2        model is utilized for each customer class instead of the load factor method used in

 3        the Base Period. SPS witness John M. Goodenough discusses load research and the

 4        SPS forecast in more detail in his testimony.

 5   Q.   Why does SPS allocate demand costs using a 12-CP approach?

 6   A.   SPS uses demand allocation factors for costs that are a function of a utility requiring

 7        the capacity to be ready and available at all times to provide service for the

 8        generation and transmission of electricity among its customer jurisdictions. The

 9        use of the 12-CP methodology, which is a common industry practice, ensures that

10        investment in generation and transmission capacity and O&M expense are allocated

11        among jurisdictions by the capacity required to provide those services to each

12        jurisdiction—i.e., based on that jurisdiction’s proportional use of capacity at the

13        time of peak system demands throughout the year. In addition, because SPS is a

14        multi-jurisdictional utility, the method of determining cost responsibility across

15        those jurisdictions must be consistent so that the combination of costs applicable to

16        each jurisdiction is not under- or overstated. This is accomplished by employing

17        the 12-CP methodology.

11        wholesale jurisdiction?

12   A.   Demand or capacity-related costs are also allocated using a 12-CP demand

13        allocation factor at FERC for SPS’s wholesale jurisdiction.

14   Q.   How are production energy costs allocated among SPS’s jurisdictions?

15   A.   SPS allocates production energy costs among SPS’s jurisdictions based upon the

16        ratio of forecasted energy consumption during the FTY in each jurisdiction,

17        adjusted for line losses, to the total SPS system energy forecast for the 12 months

18        ending November 30, 2027. It is appropriate to allocate variable energy costs on

19        that basis because energy is a measure of metered consumption over time

5    A.   Yes. SPS’s method for allocating production non-fuel energy costs was applied in

 1                           IV.     CLASS COST OF SERVICE STUDY

 2   Q.      What do you address in this section of your testimony?

 3   A.      I discuss the CCOSS, which accomplishes the following: (1) functionalizes New

 4           Mexico retail costs to the electric utility functions necessary for SPS to provide

 7           requirement among the New Mexico retail customer classes based upon how each

 8           class causes those costs to be incurred.

 9   Q.      Please summarize what the CCOSS presents.

10   A.      In addition to the functionalization, classification, and allocation of the proposed

11           New Mexico retail revenue requirement, the CCOSS compares the recovery of

12           costs under present rates from each customer class to the cost to provide service to

13           each customer class which is displayed the revenue deficiency.

10   Q.   What are the primary factors that can drive differences in the results of a

11        CCOSS between rate proceedings?

12   A.   Changes in how customer classes use the utility’s system throughout the year, load

13        growth or load loss in customer classes, changes in the relationship of how each

14        customer class uses the utility’s system compared to other customer classes, and

15        changes in the relationship of FTY costs among the utility’s functions in providing

17        factors in this case are load growth among the Commercial and Industrial customer

18        classes and increased costs assigned to the NM retail jurisdiction.
